1: //! Canonical design-token conventions (spec/TOKENS.md), shared with the
2: //! TypeScript DOM client: the Rust renderer consumes these tables directly, and
3: //! `pathland-ts-codegen` emits the TS equivalents from them — so the
4: //! `--pl-*` naming, the `dark.` scheme prefix, the generative `space.<N>`
5: //! family, and the length-token rules cannot drift between the renderers.
6: 
7: /// The scheme prefix stripped when naming a CSS variable (`dark.color.primary`
8: /// overrides the same `--pl-color-primary` inside a dark media query).
9: pub const DARK_PREFIX: &str = "dark.";
10: 
11: /// The CSS custom-property prefix for every token variable.
12: pub const VAR_PREFIX: &str = "--pl-";
13: 
14: /// Prefix for the **explicit dark-value** variable family. Every canonical token
15: /// also exposes its dark-layer value at `--pl-dark-<path>` regardless of the
16: /// active scheme, so a `dark.`-prefixed reference can force the dark value
17: /// (spec/TOKENS.md).
18: pub const FORCED_DARK_VAR_PREFIX: &str = "--pl-dark-";
19: 
20: /// The generative spacing family: `space.<N>` resolves to
21: /// `calc(var(--pl-space-base) * N)`.
22: pub const SPACE_FAMILY: &str = "space.";
23: 
24: /// Token paths whose F32 values are CSS lengths (emitted with `px`): the value
25: /// renders with a `px` suffix when it matches any of these leading prefixes.
26: pub const LENGTH_PREFIXES: &[&str] = &[
27:     "space.",
28:     "radius.",
29:     "border.width.",
30:     "size.control.",
31:     "control.padding.",
32:     "control.height.",
33: ];
34: 
35: /// Prefix/suffix length rules: a path matching `prefix…suffix` is a length.
36: pub const LENGTH_PREFIX_SUFFIX: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
37:     ("control.font.", ".size"),
38:     ("font.heading.", ".size"),
39: ];
40: 
41: /// Exact-length token paths.
42: pub const LENGTH_EXACT: &[&str] = &["font.body.size", "font.caption.size"];
43: 
44: /// `elevation.<low|high>.<component>`: these suffixes are lengths.
45: pub const LENGTH_ELEVATION_SUFFIXES: &[&str] = &[".radius", ".x", ".y", ".blur"];
46: 
47: /// Characters preserved verbatim in a CSS variable name; every other character
48: /// maps to `-`. (ASCII alphanumerics plus `-` and `_`.)
49: pub const VAR_NAME_PRESERVED: &str = "alphanumeric, '-', '_'";

1: # Pathland Design Tokens
2: 
3: **Status:** Draft
4: **Last Updated:** October 27, 2026
5: 
6: ---
7: 
8: ## Purpose
9: 
10: Design tokens are the application-facing vocabulary for **look and feel** —
11: colors, typography, spacing, radii (roundings), border widths, elevations, and
12: control styling. They let an application **roll a full theme** — including a
13: **dark variant** — that is honored consistently across every renderer, while
14: leaving platform-native defaults and interaction-state styling to the renderer.
15: 
16: This document is the companion catalog for the [Design Token
17: System](./OPCODE.md#design-token-system). It defines:
18: 
19: - the **standard token catalog** (what renderers must understand),
20: - the **resolution contract** (override → default → parent → fallback),
21: - the **color-scheme contract** (base = light, `dark.` = dark), and
22: - the **renderer integration contract** (how future native renderers adopt it).
23: 
24: The wire encoding (`PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`, the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type)
25: lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md). Modifier mapping lives in
26: [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md). The DSL surface is specified in
27: [DSL.md](./DSL.md).
28: 
29: > **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
30: > in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. This document
31: > defines the protocol contract only.
32: 
33: ---
34: 
35: ## Core Principle
36: 
37: > **The application owns the theme. The renderer owns the defaults, the scheme
38: > detection, and the interaction states.**
39: 
40: - The **application** declares a theme: token overrides (base values = the
41:   **light** design, `dark.`-prefixed values = the **dark** design) and, in a
42:   style property, a **token reference** instead of a literal value.
43: - The **renderer** supplies platform-appropriate defaults for the standard
44:   catalog (both light and dark), derives the **effective color scheme** from the
45:   platform (OS / browser / native theme), resolves token references, and owns
46:   hover/pressed/focus/disabled styling.
47: 
48: This preserves native look-and-feel by default and gives the application
49: cross-renderer consistency when it overrides tokens.
50: 
51: ### Ownership
52: 
53: | Aspect | Owner |
54: |--------|-------|
55: | Theme values (base + `dark.*`) | Application |
56: | Color-scheme detection (light/dark) | Renderer (platform-derived; app may force via `SET_COLOR_SCHEME`) |
57: | Default token values (light + dark) | Renderer |
58: | Token resolution (override → default → parent → fallback) | Renderer |
59: | Interaction states (hover/pressed/focus/disabled) | Renderer |
60: | Literal property values | Application |
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ## Token Identification
65: 
66: Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** — `color.primary`,
67: `font.body.size`, `space.2` — case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. A `dark.`
68: prefix selects the **dark variant** of a token (`dark.color.primary`).
69: 
70: The path namespace is **open**: the standard catalog below is a contract the
71: renderer MUST implement; any path outside it is **application-defined** and
72: renderer-optional (the renderer falls back rather than erroring).
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## Value Types
77: 
78: A token's value uses the standard [value types](./OPCODE.md#value-types) —
79: `COLOR` (packed `0xAARRGGBB`, sRGB), `F32`, `U32`, `I32`, `U8`, `STRING`, `ENUM`.
80: 
81: A **token reference** in a property uses the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`):
82: `C` = arenaRef to the token path. A property carries **exactly one** value —
83: either a literal (`COLOR`/`F32`/…) or a token reference, never both (see
84: [References in properties](#references-in-properties)).
85: 
86: ---
87: 
88: ## Standard Token Catalog
89: 
90: The catalog is layered. **Tier 1 (core)** tokens are mandatory: a renderer MUST
91: provide light and dark defaults and resolve them. **Tier 2 (extended)** tokens
92: are recommended: a renderer SHOULD provide defaults, and an application MAY
93: override them; a renderer that cannot apply a Tier 2 token ignores it (the same
94: "allowed and ignored" rule as unapplicable modifiers).
95: 
96: Default values are **renderer-owned and platform-appropriate**; the tables below
97: name the tokens and their *meaning*, never concrete values. The renderer MUST
98: resolve tokens by name and MAY map them onto native semantic resources (e.g. the
99: platform's system text color for `color.text.primary`).
100: 
101: ### Colors — Tier 1
102: 
103: | Token | Meaning |
104: |-------|---------|
105: | `color.primary` | Primary brand / accent fill |
106: | `color.secondary` | Secondary brand / accent fill |
107: | `color.background` | Document / canvas background |
108: | `color.surface` | Raised surface (cards, panels, popovers) |
109: | `color.text.primary` | Primary text color |
110: | `color.text.secondary` | Secondary / muted text color |
111: | `color.text.onPrimary` | Text placed on a `color.primary` fill |
112: | `color.border` | Default border / outline color |
113: | `color.accent` | Accent for controls (focus, selection, toggle fill) |
114: 
115: Tier 2: `color.separator` (hairline dividers), and status colors
116: `color.success`, `color.warning`, `color.danger`, `color.info`.
117: 
118: ### Typography — Tier 1 core
119: 
120: | Token | Meaning |
121: |-------|---------|
122: | `font.body.size` | Body text size |
123: | `font.body.weight` | Body text weight (100–900) |
124: | `font.body.family` | Body font family (STRING) |
125: 
126: Tier 2: `font.body.lineHeight`, `font.caption.size`,
127: `font.heading.1.size`–`font.heading.6.size` (with matching `.weight`/`.family`
128: paths), `font.mono.family`.
129: 
130: The **predefined typographies** (`TEXT_STYLE`: `LargeTitle`…`Caption2`,
131: spec/MODIFIERS.md §2) are the semantic counterparts of these token paths: the
132: renderer owns their concrete size/weight (a baked per-renderer HIG scale). An
133: application that wants full control can instead bind text to a `TEXT_STYLE` of
134: its own via the `font.<style>.*` token paths above, or set an explicit
135: `FONT_SIZE`/`FONT_WEIGHT`/`FONT_FAMILY` override on top.
136: 
137: ### Spacing — Tier 1
138: 
139: Spacing is a **generative family** (Tailwind-v4 style): one base unit
140: multiplied by an arbitrary number.
141: 
142: | Token | Meaning |
143: |-------|---------|
144: | `space.base` | The spacing **unit** (F32) — override this to change the whole density |
145: | `space.<N>` | `space.base` × N, where N is any positive decimal (`space.1`, `space.2`, `space.0.5`, `space.3.75`) — **computed** by the resolver |
146: 
147: Rules:
148: 
149: 1. The `space.<N>` family is **generative**, not independently valued: the
150:    renderer resolves `space.base` and multiplies by the numeric leaf. Individual
151:    members MUST NOT be overridden via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` — override `space.base`
152:    to control the whole scale.
153: 2. The color-scheme layer and parent fallback apply to `space.base`, never to an
154:    individual `space.<N>` member (`dark.space.2` is not a token; the dark layer
155:    is `dark.space.base`).
156: 3. A spacing/padding property MAY carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to any
157:    `space.<N>` path — e.g. a DSL expresses `.padding(space.2)` or `Space(2)`.
158:    Literal F32 spacing values remain valid and unthemed.
159: 
160: Tier 2: `size.control.xs` / `sm` / `md` / `lg` — standard control heights.
161: 
162: ### Radius (roundings) — Tier 1
163: 
164: | Token | Meaning |
165: |-------|---------|
166: | `radius.xs` / `radius.sm` / `radius.md` / `radius.lg` / `radius.xl` | Corner radius scale (F32) |
167: | `radius.full` | Fully round (pill/circle) — renderer resolves to its "infinite" value |
168: 
169: ### Borders — Tier 1 core
170: 
171: | Token | Meaning |
172: |-------|---------|
173: | `border.width.thin` | Default hairline/border width |
174: 
175: Tier 2: `border.width.thick`.
176: 
177: ### Elevation — Tier 2
178: 
179: Shadows are composite; each component is its own token:
180: 
181: | Token | Meaning |
182: |-------|---------|
183: | `elevation.low.color` / `radius` / `x` / `y` / `blur` | Low elevation shadow |
184: | `elevation.high.color` / `radius` / `x` / `y` / `blur` | High elevation shadow |
185: 
186: ### Opacity — Tier 2
187: 
188: | Token | Meaning |
189: |-------|---------|
190: | `opacity.disabled` | The renderer MAY apply this to disabled controls. The disabled **state** itself is the `ENABLED` property; its visual handling (including this opacity) remains renderer-owned. |
191: 
192: ### Shared control core — Tier 1
193: 
194: Tokens every control-style component (buttons, inputs, switches, sliders, …)
195: shares. Renderers MUST resolve these; an individual token a renderer cannot
196: apply is ignored.
197: 
198: | Token | Meaning |
199: |-------|---------|
200: | `control.background` | Control resting background |
201: | `control.foreground` | Control content (label/icon) color |
202: | `control.border` | Control border color |
203: | `control.border.width` | Control border width |
204: | `control.radius` | Control corner radius |
205: | `control.padding.horizontal` / `control.padding.vertical` | Control inner padding |
206: | `control.height` | Control height (F32) |
207: | `control.font.size` / `control.font.weight` | Control text |
208: | `control.accent` | Control accent (fill, selection, focus) |
209: 
210: ### Per-component tokens
211: 
212: Small sets; only where a component's semantics genuinely differ from
213: `control.*`. All Tier 1 unless noted.
214: 
215: **Buttons** (Tier 1): `button.background`, `button.foreground`, `button.border`,
216: `button.radius`, `button.padding`, `button.height`, `button.font.size`,
217: `button.font.weight`, `button.accent`.
218: 
219: > A composite shorthand such as `button.padding` (two-axis) is renderer-owned:
220: > the scalar token value types cannot encode a multi-part CSS shorthand. Apps
221: > that need a scalar override should use the shared control padding tokens or
222: > per-component properties.
223: 
224: **Text fields / editors** (Tier 1): `input.background`, `input.foreground`,
225: `input.placeholder`, `input.border`, `input.radius`, `input.font.size`.
226: 
227: **Toggle / switch** (Tier 1): `toggle.accent`, `toggle.track.off`,
228: `toggle.track.on`, `toggle.thumb`.
229: 
230: **Slider** (Tier 1): `slider.accent`, `slider.track`, `slider.thumb`.
231: 
232: **Progress / gauge** (Tier 1): `progress.track`, `progress.fill`,
233: `gauge.track`, `gauge.fill`.
234: 
235: **Stepper** (Tier 2): `stepper.accent`, `stepper.background`, `stepper.border`,
236: `stepper.radius`.
237: 
238: **Picker** (Tier 2): `picker.accent`, `picker.background`, `picker.border`,
239: `picker.radius`.
240: 
241: **Menu** (Tier 2): `menu.background`, `menu.foreground`, `menu.border`,
242: `menu.radius`.
243: 
244: **Label** (Tier 2): `label.foreground`, `label.font.size`.
245: 
246: ---
247: 
248: ## Color Schemes (Light / Dark)
249: 
250: Base token paths define the **light** design. A `dark.`-prefixed path defines
251: the **dark** design for the same token.
252: 
253: The renderer derives the **effective color scheme** from its platform's native
254: light/dark signal by default. An application MAY override it for the whole host
255: with `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` (`platform` / `light` / `dark`); the renderer
256: applies the override until the application restores `platform`. The
257: platform-derived signal itself is never carried by the protocol.
258: 
259: ### Rules
260: 
261: 1. **Base = light.** `color.primary` is the light value; `dark.color.primary`
262:    is the dark value.
263: 2. A renderer MUST provide **both** light and dark defaults for every Tier 1
264:    token (platform-appropriate). Dark mode therefore works even when the
265:    application only overrides base tokens.
266: 3. The application rolls a full theme by overriding base values and — where the
267:    dark look must differ — `dark.*` values.
268: 4. The renderer MUST **re-resolve** every token-referencing property when the
269:    effective scheme changes (including a `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` override), and MAY
270:    animate the transition.
271: 5. A **`DESIGN_TOKEN` reference** whose path starts with `dark.` is an
272:    **explicit dark-variant reference**: it resolves the bare path against the
273:    dark layer regardless of the active scheme. (A `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` override
274:    still uses the `dark.` prefix to select the dark layer.)
275: 6. The `dark.` prefix is the first scheme prefix; the namespace is open so
276:    custom schemes could follow. Only `light` (base) and `dark` are
277:    standardized.
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## Resolution
282: 
283: ```
284: FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath, scheme):
285:     # Walk most-specific → least-specific, applying the dark layer first.
286:     layers = []
287:     if scheme == dark:
288:         layers += [dark.path, dark.parent(path), …dark.root]   # dark.* layer
289:     layers += [path, parent(path), …root]                       # base layer
290: 
291:     for candidate in layers:
292:         if appOverrides.has(candidate):
293:             return appOverrides[candidate]
294:     for candidate in layers:
295:         if rendererDefaults.has(candidate):
296:             return rendererDefaults[candidate]
297:     return fallbackValue(path)
298: ```
299: 
300: Example — `color.primary` with the **dark** scheme active and only
301: `dark.color.primary` overridden:
302: 
303: 1. `dark.color.primary` — app override → **used**.
304: 2. (Unreached) `color.primary` app override, `dark.color.primary` renderer
305:    default, etc.
306: 
307: With the **light** scheme active:
308: 
309: 1. `color.primary` — app override, else renderer default, else parent/fallback.
310:    The `dark.*` layer is skipped entirely.
311: 
312: ### Generative token families
313: 
314: A **generative family** is a token rule rather than an independent value. Today
315: the `space` family is generative: `space.<N>` resolves by resolving `space.base`
316: (the scheme layer and parent fallback apply there) and multiplying by the
317: numeric leaf parsed from the path. This lets one override (`space.base`) drive
318: an arbitrarily fine spacing scale without per-step tokens. Only the `space`
319: family is generative today; other families could follow.
320: 
321: ---
322: 
323: ## References in properties
324: 
325: Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY instead
326: carry the **`DESIGN_TOKEN`** value type (`0x08`), with `C` = arenaRef to the
327: token path. The renderer resolves the reference against the token tables and the
328: current scheme, and re-resolves when the scheme changes.
329: 
330: - This is how a DSL expresses *semantic intent*: `.foregroundStyle(.primary)`
331:   or `Color.token("color.primary")` emits a token reference, not a packed color.
332: - A literal value and a token reference are mutually exclusive on a property.
333: - Because overrides and the scheme are renderer state, a token-typed property
334:   requires **no re-emission** when a token changes — the renderer re-resolves.
335: - If a reference cannot be resolved (no override, no renderer default), the
336:   property is **left unset** and the renderer's own default styling applies;
337:   resolution NEVER errors and MUST NOT retain a previously resolved value.
338: - `META::RESET_THEME` clears every application override (base + `dark.*`) and
339:   re-resolves all token-referencing properties against the renderer defaults.
340:   A replacement theme is emitted as `RESET_THEME` followed by its
341:   `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in the same frame.
342: 
343: ---
344: 
345: ## Renderer Responsibilities
346: 
347: A renderer MUST:
348: 
349: 1. Provide platform-appropriate **light and dark defaults** for all Tier 1
350:    tokens.
351: 2. Accept `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides, and clear
352:    them on `META::RESET_THEME`.
353: 3. Derive the effective color scheme from the platform (or honor
354:    `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME`) and re-resolve on change.
355: 4. Resolve token references (`DESIGN_TOKEN` value type) in properties, including
356:    explicit `dark.` references.
357: 5. Fall back to defaults when no override exists; leave the property unset when
358:    the reference cannot be resolved.
359: 6. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.
360: 
361: A renderer MAY:
362: 
363: - Map tokens onto native semantic resources (system colors, platform
364:   typography) for its defaults.
365: - **Ignore** individual tokens it cannot apply (Tier 2, or Tier 1 tokens
366:   without a native equivalent) — the "allowed and ignored" rule modifiers use.
367: - Quantize / approximate token values to platform capabilities (e.g. RGB565
368:   color depth on embedded displays, limited font sets).
369: 
370: An application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (base and `dark.*`)
371: and reference any token in a property; it MUST NOT assume specific default
372: values.
373: 
374: ---
375: 
376: ## Renderer Integration Contract
377: 
378: A future native renderer adopts the token system by implementing five pieces:
379: 
380: 1. **Default token table** — Tier 1 light + dark defaults from native resources.
381: 2. **Scheme detection** — the platform's native light/dark signal.
382: 3. **Resolution** — the override → default → parent → fallback algorithm, with
383:    the `dark.*` layer keyed on the effective scheme.
384: 4. **Property resolution** — any property carrying a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference
385:    resolves to the concrete native value (e.g. a dynamic system color / theme
386:    resource / style value).
387: 5. **Re-resolution** — on scheme change, re-resolve and update the rendered
388:    output; animate if native.
389: 
390: The same contract powers the reference renderers (`pathland-render-html`,
391: `pathland-render-gtk`, the JS DOM renderer) and is checked in their `status.md`
392: files.

# Pathland Design Tokens

**Status:** Draft
**Last Updated:** October 27, 2026

---

## Purpose

Design tokens are the application-facing vocabulary for **look and feel** —
colors, typography, spacing, radii (roundings), border widths, elevations, and
control styling. They let an application **roll a full theme** — including a
**dark variant** — that is honored consistently across every renderer, while
leaving platform-native defaults and interaction-state styling to the renderer.

This document is the companion catalog for the [Design Token
System](./OPCODE.md#design-token-system). It defines:

- the **standard token catalog** (what renderers must understand),
- the **resolution contract** (override → default → parent → fallback),
- the **color-scheme contract** (base = light, `dark.` = dark), and
- the **renderer integration contract** (how future native renderers adopt it).

The wire encoding (`PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`, the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type)
lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md). Modifier mapping lives in
[MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md). The DSL surface is specified in
[DSL.md](./DSL.md).

> **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
> in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. This document
> defines the protocol contract only.

---

## Core Principle

> **The application owns the theme. The renderer owns the defaults, the scheme
> detection, and the interaction states.**

- The **application** declares a theme: token overrides (base values = the
  **light** design, `dark.`-prefixed values = the **dark** design) and, in a
  style property, a **token reference** instead of a literal value.
- The **renderer** supplies platform-appropriate defaults for the standard
  catalog (both light and dark), derives the **effective color scheme** from the
  platform (OS / browser / native theme), resolves token references, and owns
  hover/pressed/focus/disabled styling.

This preserves native look-and-feel by default and gives the application
cross-renderer consistency when it overrides tokens.

### Ownership

| Aspect | Owner |
|--------|-------|
| Theme values (base + `dark.*`) | Application |
| Color-scheme detection (light/dark) | Renderer (platform-derived; app may force via `SET_COLOR_SCHEME`) |
| Default token values (light + dark) | Renderer |
| Token resolution (override → default → parent → fallback) | Renderer |
| Interaction states (hover/pressed/focus/disabled) | Renderer |
| Literal property values | Application |

---

## Token Identification

Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** — `color.primary`,
`font.body.size`, `space.2` — case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. A `dark.`
prefix selects the **dark variant** of a token (`dark.color.primary`).

The path namespace is **open**: the standard catalog below is a contract the
renderer MUST implement; any path outside it is **application-defined** and
renderer-optional (the renderer falls back rather than erroring).

---

## Value Types

A token's value uses the standard [value types](./OPCODE.md#value-types) —
`COLOR` (packed `0xAARRGGBB`, sRGB), `F32`, `U32`, `I32`, `U8`, `STRING`, `ENUM`.

A **token reference** in a property uses the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`):
`C` = arenaRef to the token path. A property carries **exactly one** value —
either a literal (`COLOR`/`F32`/…) or a token reference, never both (see
[References in properties](#references-in-properties)).

---

## Standard Token Catalog

The catalog is layered. **Tier 1 (core)** tokens are mandatory: a renderer MUST
provide light and dark defaults and resolve them. **Tier 2 (extended)** tokens
are recommended: a renderer SHOULD provide defaults, and an application MAY
override them; a renderer that cannot apply a Tier 2 token ignores it (the same
"allowed and ignored" rule as unapplicable modifiers).

Default values are **renderer-owned and platform-appropriate**; the tables below
name the tokens and their *meaning*, never concrete values. The renderer MUST
resolve tokens by name and MAY map them onto native semantic resources (e.g. the
platform's system text color for `color.text.primary`).

### Colors — Tier 1

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `color.primary` | Primary brand / accent fill |
| `color.secondary` | Secondary brand / accent fill |
| `color.background` | Document / canvas background |
| `color.surface` | Raised surface (cards, panels, popovers) |
| `color.text.primary` | Primary text color |
| `color.text.secondary` | Secondary / muted text color |
| `color.text.onPrimary` | Text placed on a `color.primary` fill |
| `color.border` | Default border / outline color |
| `color.accent` | Accent for controls (focus, selection, toggle fill) |

Tier 2: `color.separator` (hairline dividers), and status colors
`color.success`, `color.warning`, `color.danger`, `color.info`.

### Typography — Tier 1 core

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `font.body.size` | Body text size |
| `font.body.weight` | Body text weight (100–900) |
| `font.body.family` | Body font family (STRING) |

Tier 2: `font.body.lineHeight`, `font.caption.size`,
`font.heading.1.size`–`font.heading.6.size` (with matching `.weight`/`.family`
paths), `font.mono.family`.

The **predefined typographies** (`TEXT_STYLE`: `LargeTitle`…`Caption2`,
spec/MODIFIERS.md §2) are the semantic counterparts of these token paths: the
renderer owns their concrete size/weight (a baked per-renderer HIG scale). An
application that wants full control can instead bind text to a `TEXT_STYLE` of
its own via the `font.<style>.*` token paths above, or set an explicit
`FONT_SIZE`/`FONT_WEIGHT`/`FONT_FAMILY` override on top.

### Spacing — Tier 1

Spacing is a **generative family** (Tailwind-v4 style): one base unit
multiplied by an arbitrary number.

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `space.base` | The spacing **unit** (F32) — override this to change the whole density |
| `space.<N>` | `space.base` × N, where N is any positive decimal (`space.1`, `space.2`, `space.0.5`, `space.3.75`) — **computed** by the resolver |

Rules:

1. The `space.<N>` family is **generative**, not independently valued: the
   renderer resolves `space.base` and multiplies by the numeric leaf. Individual
   members MUST NOT be overridden via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` — override `space.base`
   to control the whole scale.
2. The color-scheme layer and parent fallback apply to `space.base`, never to an
   individual `space.<N>` member (`dark.space.2` is not a token; the dark layer
   is `dark.space.base`).
3. A spacing/padding property MAY carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to any
   `space.<N>` path — e.g. a DSL expresses `.padding(space.2)` or `Space(2)`.
   Literal F32 spacing values remain valid and unthemed.

Tier 2: `size.control.xs` / `sm` / `md` / `lg` — standard control heights.

### Radius (roundings) — Tier 1

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `radius.xs` / `radius.sm` / `radius.md` / `radius.lg` / `radius.xl` | Corner radius scale (F32) |
| `radius.full` | Fully round (pill/circle) — renderer resolves to its "infinite" value |

### Borders — Tier 1 core

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `border.width.thin` | Default hairline/border width |

Tier 2: `border.width.thick`.

### Elevation — Tier 2

Shadows are composite; each component is its own token:

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `elevation.low.color` / `radius` / `x` / `y` / `blur` | Low elevation shadow |
| `elevation.high.color` / `radius` / `x` / `y` / `blur` | High elevation shadow |

### Opacity — Tier 2

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `opacity.disabled` | The renderer MAY apply this to disabled controls. The disabled **state** itself is the `ENABLED` property; its visual handling (including this opacity) remains renderer-owned. |

### Shared control core — Tier 1

Tokens every control-style component (buttons, inputs, switches, sliders, …)
shares. Renderers MUST resolve these; an individual token a renderer cannot
apply is ignored.

| Token | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `control.background` | Control resting background |
| `control.foreground` | Control content (label/icon) color |
| `control.border` | Control border color |
| `control.border.width` | Control border width |
| `control.radius` | Control corner radius |
| `control.padding.horizontal` / `control.padding.vertical` | Control inner padding |
| `control.height` | Control height (F32) |
| `control.font.size` / `control.font.weight` | Control text |
| `control.accent` | Control accent (fill, selection, focus) |

### Per-component tokens

Small sets; only where a component's semantics genuinely differ from
`control.*`. All Tier 1 unless noted.

**Buttons** (Tier 1): `button.background`, `button.foreground`, `button.border`,
`button.radius`, `button.padding`, `button.height`, `button.font.size`,
`button.font.weight`, `button.accent`.

> A composite shorthand such as `button.padding` (two-axis) is renderer-owned:
> the scalar token value types cannot encode a multi-part CSS shorthand. Apps
> that need a scalar override should use the shared control padding tokens or
> per-component properties.

**Text fields / editors** (Tier 1): `input.background`, `input.foreground`,
`input.placeholder`, `input.border`, `input.radius`, `input.font.size`.

**Toggle / switch** (Tier 1): `toggle.accent`, `toggle.track.off`,
`toggle.track.on`, `toggle.thumb`.

**Slider** (Tier 1): `slider.accent`, `slider.track`, `slider.thumb`.

**Progress / gauge** (Tier 1): `progress.track`, `progress.fill`,
`gauge.track`, `gauge.fill`.

**Stepper** (Tier 2): `stepper.accent`, `stepper.background`, `stepper.border`,
`stepper.radius`.

**Picker** (Tier 2): `picker.accent`, `picker.background`, `picker.border`,
`picker.radius`.

**Menu** (Tier 2): `menu.background`, `menu.foreground`, `menu.border`,
`menu.radius`.

**Label** (Tier 2): `label.foreground`, `label.font.size`.

---

## Color Schemes (Light / Dark)

Base token paths define the **light** design. A `dark.`-prefixed path defines
the **dark** design for the same token.

The renderer derives the **effective color scheme** from its platform's native
light/dark signal by default. An application MAY override it for the whole host
with `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` (`platform` / `light` / `dark`); the renderer
applies the override until the application restores `platform`. The
platform-derived signal itself is never carried by the protocol.

### Rules

1. **Base = light.** `color.primary` is the light value; `dark.color.primary`
   is the dark value.
2. A renderer MUST provide **both** light and dark defaults for every Tier 1
   token (platform-appropriate). Dark mode therefore works even when the
   application only overrides base tokens.
3. The application rolls a full theme by overriding base values and — where the
   dark look must differ — `dark.*` values.
4. The renderer MUST **re-resolve** every token-referencing property when the
   effective scheme changes (including a `SET_COLOR_SCHEME` override), and MAY
   animate the transition.
5. A **`DESIGN_TOKEN` reference** whose path starts with `dark.` is an
   **explicit dark-variant reference**: it resolves the bare path against the
   dark layer regardless of the active scheme. (A `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` override
   still uses the `dark.` prefix to select the dark layer.)
6. The `dark.` prefix is the first scheme prefix; the namespace is open so
   custom schemes could follow. Only `light` (base) and `dark` are
   standardized.

---

## Resolution

```
FUNCTION resolveToken(tokenPath, scheme):
    # Walk most-specific → least-specific, applying the dark layer first.
    layers = []
    if scheme == dark:
        layers += [dark.path, dark.parent(path), …dark.root]   # dark.* layer
    layers += [path, parent(path), …root]                       # base layer

    for candidate in layers:
        if appOverrides.has(candidate):
            return appOverrides[candidate]
    for candidate in layers:
        if rendererDefaults.has(candidate):
            return rendererDefaults[candidate]
    return fallbackValue(path)
```

Example — `color.primary` with the **dark** scheme active and only
`dark.color.primary` overridden:

1. `dark.color.primary` — app override → **used**.
2. (Unreached) `color.primary` app override, `dark.color.primary` renderer
   default, etc.

With the **light** scheme active:

1. `color.primary` — app override, else renderer default, else parent/fallback.
   The `dark.*` layer is skipped entirely.

### Generative token families

A **generative family** is a token rule rather than an independent value. Today
the `space` family is generative: `space.<N>` resolves by resolving `space.base`
(the scheme layer and parent fallback apply there) and multiplying by the
numeric leaf parsed from the path. This lets one override (`space.base`) drive
an arbitrarily fine spacing scale without per-step tokens. Only the `space`
family is generative today; other families could follow.

---

## References in properties

Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY instead
carry the **`DESIGN_TOKEN`** value type (`0x08`), with `C` = arenaRef to the
token path. The renderer resolves the reference against the token tables and the
current scheme, and re-resolves when the scheme changes.

- This is how a DSL expresses *semantic intent*: `.foregroundStyle(.primary)`
  or `Color.token("color.primary")` emits a token reference, not a packed color.
- A literal value and a token reference are mutually exclusive on a property.
- Because overrides and the scheme are renderer state, a token-typed property
  requires **no re-emission** when a token changes — the renderer re-resolves.
- If a reference cannot be resolved (no override, no renderer default), the
  property is **left unset** and the renderer's own default styling applies;
  resolution NEVER errors and MUST NOT retain a previously resolved value.
- `META::RESET_THEME` clears every application override (base + `dark.*`) and
  re-resolves all token-referencing properties against the renderer defaults.
  A replacement theme is emitted as `RESET_THEME` followed by its
  `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in the same frame.

---

## Renderer Responsibilities

A renderer MUST:

1. Provide platform-appropriate **light and dark defaults** for all Tier 1
   tokens.
2. Accept `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides, and clear
   them on `META::RESET_THEME`.
3. Derive the effective color scheme from the platform (or honor
   `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME`) and re-resolve on change.
4. Resolve token references (`DESIGN_TOKEN` value type) in properties, including
   explicit `dark.` references.
5. Fall back to defaults when no override exists; leave the property unset when
   the reference cannot be resolved.
6. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.

A renderer MAY:

- Map tokens onto native semantic resources (system colors, platform
  typography) for its defaults.
- **Ignore** individual tokens it cannot apply (Tier 2, or Tier 1 tokens
  without a native equivalent) — the "allowed and ignored" rule modifiers use.
- Quantize / approximate token values to platform capabilities (e.g. RGB565
  color depth on embedded displays, limited font sets).

An application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (base and `dark.*`)
and reference any token in a property; it MUST NOT assume specific default
values.

---

## Renderer Integration Contract

A future native renderer adopts the token system by implementing five pieces:

1. **Default token table** — Tier 1 light + dark defaults from native resources.
2. **Scheme detection** — the platform's native light/dark signal.
3. **Resolution** — the override → default → parent → fallback algorithm, with
   the `dark.*` layer keyed on the effective scheme.
4. **Property resolution** — any property carrying a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference
   resolves to the concrete native value (e.g. a dynamic system color / theme
   resource / style value).
5. **Re-resolution** — on scheme change, re-resolve and update the rendered
   output; animate if native.

The same contract powers the reference renderers (`pathland-render-html`,
`pathland-render-gtk`, the JS DOM renderer) and is checked in their `status.md`
files.

# pathland-render-html (Rust) — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 27, 2026

The **server-side / remote-projection HTML renderer**: a **stateless, streaming**
pure function of the opcode stream producing declarative HTML. Each render call
decodes a self-contained snapshot batch into a **transient** map, walks it once,
and emits HTML text out — no retained tree, zero cross-call state (Renderer
Statelessness). Protocol contract: `spec/`.

## Implemented

- **`PROXY_VIEW` (0x1E)**: renders as a plain container box (a flex column,
  like a stack with one child) and lays out the (id-remapped) origin subtree the
  proxying server spliced in — the renderer holds no notion of "remote"
  (spec/PROXY.md §5). Without this arm the component fell to the `_ => String::new()`
  default and the spliced subtree was dropped. Covered by a unit test.
- **Stateless streaming API**: `HtmlRenderer::render_document(opcodes, strings, root)`
  / `render_fragment(...)` build a transient decode map per call and stream HTML;
  the retained `apply`/`apply_frame`/`render` model is removed.

And how tokens override is wired from Java (SET_DESIGN_TOKEN). The user wants "shift the base design for html renderer. Not just by overrides." This likely means: change the entire base design system (the built-in CSS/tokens) rather than individually overriding tokens. So we need to find ways to plug a theme/base stylesheet into the renderer.

Options:
1. Allow injecting a custom CSS base (theme stylesheet) into render_document.
2. Make the built-in CSS a separate "base design" artifact, with multiple built-in themes.
3. A "base design" concept as a set of token defaults emitted via SET_DESIGN_TOKEN at app start. But that's "overrides."

Let me look at the Java HTML shim, server core SSR page template, and DOM client's token handling. Let me search.

# pathland-render-html (Java) — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 2, 2026

The **Java binding to the Rust HTML renderer** (`dev.pathland.render.html`) — a
thin **JNA shim** over `libpathland_render_html`. There is a **single renderer**
(the Rust crate), reused by every language; the former hand-written retained
Java renderer is removed. Protocol contract: `spec/`.

## Implemented

- **Stateless JNA shim**: `HtmlRenderer.instance()` links the Rust cdylib;
  `render(frame, root)` / `renderFragment(frame, root)` /
  `renderFullSnapshot(frame, root)` render a self-contained snapshot frame to
  HTML in one pass (no retained tree, no `applyFrame`); `pathland_html_free`
  releases native strings. Lazy-loaded; skipped (test assumption) when the dylib
  is absent from `java.library.path`.
- **Debug comments**: `renderDebug(frame, root)` / `renderFragmentDebug(...)`
  bind the Rust `pathland_html_render_debug` exports — each rendered node is
  prefixed with an HTML comment naming its component type and the modifiers
  applied (opt-in; the plain `render` output is unchanged).
- **Full Rust renderer surface** (canonical): all spec components render inline
  (structural + decorative CSS in a single `style` attribute), ARIA/event
  attributes, `IS_SECURE` → password, `TOGGLE_STYLE` variants,
  `DATE_PICKER_MODE`, and literal colors inline. The renderer injects its own
  built-in `<style>` block (preflight reset + design tokens + `.pathland-*`
  component defaults) into every document — no external CSS, no `/tailwind.css`.
- **Icon glyphs from the shared renderer**: `iconSvg(String name)` binds the
  Rust `pathland_html_icon_svg` export over the C ABI — the full inline `<svg>`
  for a canonical `ICON_NAME` (unknown/extension names → the renderer's
  fallback glyph, never null). Hosts serve `/_pathland/icons/<name>.svg` from
  it (Spring/Quarkus route a few lines in their starters), so the DOM client's
  lazy icon fetch gets the same glyph data SSR inlines from — one Rust source,
  no per-platform static icon files. `HtmlRendererTest` covers it.
- **Demos use the shim**: `SessionApp` no longer calls `applyFrame`; SSR renders
  the mount frame through `HtmlRenderer.render(sink.frame(), rootId)`. The
  renderer is compiled once at startup.
- **Text fields share one component class**: `TEXT_FIELD` inputs and `TEXT_EDITOR`
  textareas render with `class="pathland-input"` (Tailwind-style inset-outline
  styling from the Rust renderer's CSS); the copied `@pathland/dom-renderer`
  bundle (content-hashed `dom-renderer-<sha256>.js` in both demos) mirrors the
  class so delta-created fields hydrate identically.

## Removed (September 2026)

- `compileTailwind(overrideCss)` and the `pathland_tailwind_compile` binding are
  **deleted** — the renderer is inline-only now and needs no compiler. The demo
  `/tailwind.css` endpoints (`TailwindCssController` / `TailwindCssResource`)
  and the `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/tailwind.css">` in both `SessionApp`
  files are removed.

## Not implemented / gaps

- **Typography uses the platform system font stack** (`system-ui,
  -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, …`) — the Rust renderer's document head
  makes no external/webfont requests, so the demo pages render without loading
  any font files and work offline. An app can still override `font.body.family`
  via a `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` to any font it hosts.
- The shim is unaffected by the Rust renderer's September 2026 shell alignment
  (SPACER/MENU/STEPPER/GAUGE/PICKER markup now matches the DOM client's runtime
  shells); the demos' SSR output reflects the Rust renderer as-is, pinned by the
  `pathland-html-golden` conformance harness. `HtmlRendererTest` covers the
  semantic-role → element mapping (`NAVIGATION`→`<nav>`, `HEADER`→`<h2>`,
  `TEXT_STYLE` headings) and the DSL's rejection of non-semantic role codes,
  plus media rendering (a `VIDEO` surface bound to its `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` —
  native `<video controls>` + `data-pathland-controller`, the non-visual hidden
  controller shell, image `alt` from the accessibility label,
  `ContentMode Fill`→`cover`).

## Verified by

`mvn test -pl pathland-render-html` — JNA shim tests (skip when the Rust dylib
is absent); part of the non-demo reactor run on JDK 17.

Now I understand. The user wants to make it easy to shift the base design for the HTML renderer, "not just by overrides." This is a design/investigation request. I should present a plan with options and tradeoffs, and ask clarifying questions.

Let me understand what "base design" means precisely. The built-in CSS is one monolithic hardcoded `css::STYLE` containing:
- preflight reset
- :root token defaults (light/dark/forced-dark)
- component CSS (.pathland-*)

Currently the only way to change the look is `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides through the protocol (or literal inline props). But you can't:
- change component CSS rules (e.g. button shape/padding/hover behavior) other than via tokens
- swap the whole preflight/reset
- replace the token defaults wholesale (not individually)
- inject app CSS class-based styles
- provide alternative base designs (e.g. "Material", "compact", "brand X")

"Not just by overrides" suggests they want the ability to shift/replace the base design itself. Could be:
1. Custom base stylesheet injection (app-provided CSS) appended into the head.
2. Selectable built-in base theme/design preset.
3. A "base design" as data (tokens + component CSS) that can be authored outside Rust, e.g. via a CSS file loaded at build time or runtime.

We need to investigate and propose. Since we're in plan mode, I should explore a bit more: is there a spec for theming beyond tokens? Are there any issues in repo? Check docs and `spec/`. Also check the TS DOM client's base styling: does it rely entirely on SSR style block? The DOM client likely doesn't inject CSS. Let's check index.ts and whether it references data-pathland-tokens only. Also check service worker / asset server for custom css support. Search for "base design", "theme", "stylesheet" in spec and docs.

parts.text:
Now I have enough context to formulate a plan/investigation. The user asks "I want to investigate how to make it easy to shift the base design for html renderer. Not just by overrides."

Let me think through the possible architecture choices.

Current situation:
- `pathland-render-html/src/css.rs` has a monolithic `pub const STYLE: &str`.
- `render_document` injects it before token/fit styles.
- Design tokens are overridable via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (protocol-level) — this is the "overrides" path.
- There's no way to change component CSS or the reset, and no way to select a different built-in base design.
- The Java shim and C ABI expose no theming hook. `PathlandSession.renderHtml` post-processes the returned HTML only to add attributes/script.

The desired capability: "shift the base design" — i.e. swap/replace the base design system for the HTML renderer, not merely tweak token values.

Design dimensions:
1. **Base token values** (the `:root` defaults) — currently static. Could be a named design preset.
2. **Component CSS** (`.pathland-*` rules: layout of controls, hover/focus/disabled, shapes, transitions) — currently static and not token-driven entirely.
3. **Preflight/reset** — currently static.
4. **Document shell** (html/body, title, meta, script placement) — currently static.

Approaches:

A. **CSS custom-property-only theming + "theme preset" token tables.**
Make all component rules token-driven and provide multiple built-in base designs (e.g. default, compact, material). A base design is a token table applied as defaults. But the user explicitly says "not just by overrides," so this alone isn't enough unless base presets are first-class.

B. **External base stylesheet injection (custom CSS hook).**
Add `HtmlRenderer::with_stylesheet(css)` / C ABI `pathland_html_render_with_css` / Java `HtmlRenderer.render(frame, root, css)` that appends an app-provided CSS block into the head after the built-in block (or replaces it). This lets you fully restyle components, reset, and tokens. It's a renderer customization hook, not protocol. Concern: renderer statelessness is fine — CSS is a renderer config. But it's a per-render argument or renderer config.
   - Variants: append vs replace vs disable-builtin.
   - Security: CSS is trusted app config (server-side), no XSS concern if trusted; still should be raw injection or via `<link>`.

C. **Named base design presets compiled into the renderer**, selectable by config/C ABI: `pathland_html_render_preset(batch, len, root, preset)`. Presets = default, minimal, compact, etc. Applies token defaults + component CSS. Extensible via registration.

D. **Split the base design into "token layer" + "component layer" and expose both as overrideable data.** Base design = (token table, component CSS, reset). Add a runtime-configurable "design" object with a name and composition: `builtin:default`, `builtin:compact`, plus app CSS overlays. Defaults still renderer-owned; app can "shift" wholesale.

E. **Move base design to a CSS file loaded at runtime from the host**, e.g. `pathland_html_set_base_css(css)` or an asset served at `/_pathland/base.css` linked in the document. This makes it easy to iterate without rebuilding the Rust renderer. Since the renderer is often a cdylib in Java, a runtime CSS file/classpath resource is attractive. But stateless rendering + concurrency: global setter introduces cross-session state. Better as per-render argument or environment object.

F. **Protocol-level base theme selector:** A new META command (`META::SET_BASE_DESIGN`?) or a token path convention (e.g. `design.name`). But AGENTS.md says the protocol is king and app owns theme; adding a protocol command for a renderer-owned base design may be overreach and can't work for native renderers consistently. Also shifting base design differs per renderer. Probably out of scope / undesirable. Could be a renderer config, not protocol.

Key architectural tension: The contract says renderer owns defaults, app owns overrides. "Shifting the base design" means changing renderer defaults. So the cleanest conceptual model is: **base design is a renderer configuration (a "design preset"), not protocol**. The app selects a base design; the renderer still owns it. Optionally app CSS is an escape hatch.

We should investigate how the CSS is built and whether it can be split into layers to make presets easy. Let's examine the structure of css.rs more: it's one const. To make presets, we could:
- Keep the preflight + component CSS as a template that references tokens.
- Token tables as structured data (`const DEFAULT_LIGHT: &[(&str, &str)]` etc.) and generate the `:root` blocks.
- Component CSS is mostly token-driven already, but some hardcoded values (e.g. switch dimensions, slider sizes, button padding). Move these to tokens so a base design = token table + optionally component CSS.

But "not just overrides" strongly suggests they want to be able to change the actual stylesheet, e.g. to use a completely different design language (Tailwind-ish, Material, enterprise Lumen). So likely need a **stylesheet injection/replacement** hook plus **presets**.

Let me check whether the Rust HTML renderer has an existing "design"/"theme" API or config beyond tokens. Search for "design_theme", "Theme", "css". Already read lib. It's only token overrides from opcodes. So no config.

Let me consider naming and design.

Conceptual model: separate the "base design" into three layers:
1. **Reset/preflight** — structural baseline.
2. **Token defaults** — light/dark values.
3. **Component rules** — `.pathland-*` styling written against tokens.

A "base design" (or "design system preset") is a bundle of these three. The app can:
- choose a built-in preset,
- supply its own preset (CSS),
- or layer overrides (tokens today).

Implementation options:

**Option 1: Custom base CSS injection at render time (minimal, flexible).**
- Rust: `HtmlRenderer::with_extra_css(&str)` or `render_document_with_css(opcodes, strings, root, css)`. Emit app CSS in a `<style data-pathland-base>` after the built-in block. Maybe `with_builtin_css(bool)` to fully replace.
- C ABI: new `pathland_html_render_css(batch, len, root, css_ptr)` (and fragment variant). Keep old exports unchanged.
- Java: `HtmlRenderer.render(frame, root, BaseDesign)` / `PathlandApp.baseDesign()` returning a `BaseDesign` with `builtin`/`css`/`none`.
- Pros: easiest to shift the base; can express any design language; no need to tokenize every value.
- Cons: bypasses token system; app CSS can conflict with inline styles (inline wins, so app CSS can't override opcode props — probably fine); SSR/CSP considerations; duplicates DOM client behavior? The DOM client doesn't need it because it reads SSR DOM; but after hydration, the style element stays in the head, so fine. On a full resync, the server sends a fragment, and the client keeps the head style. Need to make sure a reconnect/resync doesn't lose it — it's from the initial document, so fine.
- Security: CSS injection is trusted server config. If sourced from a request/user, must sanitize; not a protocol payload.

**Option 2: Built-in named presets + token tables.**
- Refactor `css.rs` so the token defaults are tables, and component CSS references tokens (already mostly). Add `BaseDesign` enum with `Default`, `Compact`, `Minimal`, maybe `System`.
- `render_document` takes a preset (or renderer config).
- Pros: consistent across SSR/DOM, no CSS injection, app can switch design with one line.
- Cons: only works if presets are compiled in; adding a design means editing Rust; still limited to tokenizable aspects unless component CSS varies per preset.

**Option 3: Split base CSS into an overridable asset + link.**
- Emit `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/_pathland/base.css">` (or inline the built-in but allow replacement). Hosts serve the base CSS from classpath/static, so designers can iterate without Rust rebuilds.
- Java: a `BaseDesign` resource path; C ABI stays inline for Rust-native hosts.
- Pros: design iteration by CSS authors; no Rust rebuild; per-app CSS.
- Cons: additional network request (could be inlined for SSR), FOUC/ordering, cache invalidation, CSP, and app must host it. Also complicates statelessness/ABI.

**Option 4: Protocol-level base design selection.**
- New META command to select a renderer base design by name.
- Cons: violates "renderer owns defaults"; native renderers may not have the same designs; app cannot guarantee; adds protocol surface for a renderer-specific concern. Not recommended.

What does "shift the base design" mean precisely? Could be:
- Re-brand an existing app (colors/type/spacing) → token overrides suffice today (but user says not just overrides).
- Switch to a whole different component look (e.g. flat vs bordered, dense vs comfortable, rounded vs sharp, Material-like) → needs component CSS control.
- Swap the default token values for a design system (e.g. "Lumen") so apps get it without emitting hundreds of overrides → presets.
- Per-deployment custom design (customer branding) → external CSS.

I think the recommended plan is a **layered BaseDesign configuration** with two mechanisms:
1. **First-class base-design presets** (token tables + component CSS variants) compiled in, selected via renderer/host config.
2. **Custom base stylesheet hook** for anything else, appended after built-in (or replacing it), exposed through Rust, C ABI, Java, and server `PathlandApp`.

Also, to make presets actually work, **tokenize the remaining hardcoded component CSS values** (dimensions, gaps, paddings, transitions, border widths, fonts) and split `css.rs` into `reset` + `tokens(preset)` + `components`. This is the actual "make it easy" work.

- Rust renderer `HtmlRenderer { base: BaseDesign }` (stateless, `BaseDesign` clone/`&'static`).
- C ABI: pass preset id / CSS pointer, or a handle config object. Simplest: `pathland_html_render_with_options(batch, len, root, options_ptr)` or add args to existing render. To avoid breaking ABI, add new functions.
- Java: `PathlandApp.baseDesign()` (default `BaseDesign.builtin()`), passed via `PathlandSession.renderHtml` to `HtmlRenderer.render(frame, root, baseDesign)`. This makes it per-app and consistent across sessions.
- Also consider an app-level `baseDesign` for the DOM client? The DOM client only applies deltas; base CSS from SSR persists. But on `META::RESYNC` full snapshot the client does `applyFrame` in place, not re-render the head. Fine. However, if the client is used without SSR (e.g. a pure SPA), it needs a way to include the base CSS. Today the DOM client has no built-in base CSS at all — it relies on SSR. That's a gap. If we want base design to work in pure client mode, we'd need the TS client to also know the base theme/preset, or the server to always send the base CSS. Worth flagging. But maybe out of scope.

Let me verify: does the DOM client ever create `style` for component CSS? No. So a client-only mount (no SSR) would have unstyled components. That's already a gap. ## Investigation: shifting the HTML renderer's base design

### Current state

- The entire base design is one hardcoded string: `css::STYLE` (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/src/css.rs:16`). It bundles the Tailwind preflight, all `:root` token defaults (light/dark/forced-dark), and every `.pathland-*` component rule.
- `render_document` injects it unconditionally before token/fit styles (`lib.rs:1323`).
- `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` can only change **token values**; it renders as a separate `data-pathland-tokens` element (`lib.rs:1297`). Component CSS, the reset, non-tokenized dimensions, and hover/focus behavior are untouchable.
- No config surface exists today: Rust `HtmlRenderer` has only `debug_comments` (`lib.rs:1264`), the C ABI passes only batch/root/debug (`capi.rs`), the Java shim has no CSS/base parameter (`HtmlRenderer.java`), and `PathlandApp` exposes only `theme()` (`PathlandApp.java:18`).
- The TS DOM client only manages token overrides (`lib/typescript/src/tokens.ts`); it inherits the base CSS from SSR.
- Golden fixtures exercise `render_fragment`, so they are unaffected by the base CSS (good: changing it won't churn fixtures). The built-in CSS content is asserted by unit tests (`lib.rs:3901+`).

### What "shift the base design" requires

1. **Replace/choose the token defaults wholesale** (not emit 100 overrides per session).
2. **Change component CSS** (shape, density, typography, states) that tokens cannot express.
3. **Optionally replace the preflight/reset**.
4. Keep the app's existing per-session token overrides as a higher layer.

This is a **renderer configuration** concern, not a protocol concern. Putting a "base design" command in the protocol would violate "renderer owns defaults" and cannot work consistently across GTK/Qt/HTML.

### Options

| Option | What it gives | Tradeoffs |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Compiled-in base-design presets** (`BaseDesign` = reset + token table + component CSS) | One-line switch to `default`/`compact`/`bare`/brand; upgrade-safe styling contract | New designs require Rust changes |
| **B. Custom base stylesheet hook** (app CSS layered after, or replacing, the built-in block) | Full design freedom without forking; iterate in CSS | Apps can drift from the `.pathland-*` contract; CSS trust/CSP considerations |
| **C. External base stylesheet asset** (`<link>` or host-served file) | Designers iterate without rebuilding Rust/Java | Extra request, FOUC/order, caching, another host endpoint |
| **D. Protocol command to select a base design** | Cross-language uniformity | Not recommended: renderer-specific defaults, no native equivalent, expands the protocol for a renderer concern |

### Recommended architecture: A + B, with C as an optional delivery mechanism

Introduce a layered model:

```
reset/preflight  ->  base token table  ->  component CSS  ->  SET_DESIGN_TOKEN overrides  ->  fit bands
```

parts.text:
Good. There's already an asset serving mechanism `/_pathland/**` from classpath and `pathland.asset-dir` disk. So a design flow could leverage that: serve `/_pathland/theme.css` from a dev directory (e.g. `pathland.asset-dir`), and the renderer emits `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/_pathland/theme.css">` (or inline for prod).

But note: the base CSS must be present before first paint (avoid FOUC) and for SSR. A `<link>` still blocks render until loaded (browser blocks rendering on stylesheets), so FOUC is minimal. But the link is a separate request; for a dev design flow, that's actually ideal: edit CSS file → refresh → new CSS without rebuilding.

However, the user's concern is the *design system* for the HTML renderer: the `.pathland-*` component CSS and token defaults. Designers need to iterate on CSS rapidly. The ideal workflow:
1. Author the base CSS as a plain `.css` file in the repo (or an app resource).
2. The renderer uses it (either embedded at compile time for prod, or served/linked/inlined at runtime for dev).
3. Live-reload CSS (maybe via a dev server or browser extension) so no app restart.

Key architectural choice: Should the built-in CSS live in a `.css` file (with `include_str!` for production) instead of a Rust raw string? That alone improves authoring ergonomics (syntax highlighting, linting, Tailwind tooling), but still requires recompiling Rust because `include_str!` is baked in. But for design iteration, you can use a runtime override that reads the file.

Approaches for fast roundtrip:
A. **External base stylesheet linked in the document** (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="{base}/_pathland/base.css">`), served by the host from a file/classpath. In dev, the server reads from disk; in prod, serve embedded. Hot reload with a file watcher or browser refresh. This removes Rust compilation from the loop entirely.
   - For Rust-native hosts (GTK? no, HTML), the Rust `HtmlRenderer` would need to emit a link instead of inline CSS, or accept a `BaseDesign` with a `link` URL. But the C ABI can take a stylesheet URL.
   - If we want SSR self-contained (no external CSS) in production, use inline. In dev, link. Or always link with a content-hashed URL.
   - But the currently attached tokens/test expect no external stylesheets. That's a test, changeable.
B. **Runtime file loading into inline CSS**: `BaseDesign::from_file(path)` called per render (with mtime cache) in dev; `include_str!` in prod. The server reads the CSS file at request time and passes it to the renderer. Edit CSS → refresh → new inline style. No rebuild. This keeps output self-contained and avoids linking. Better CSP and no extra request. But each SSR render reads the file (cache by mtime) and includes it. Fine.
   - Host config: `pathland.base-design.file=src/main/resources/.../theme.css` in dev. In prod, default embedded.
   - For Java, `BaseDesign.fromFile(Path)` currently reads once at construction. For hot reload, add a `Supplier<String>` or `Path` that reads on each render (with mtime) or a `ReloadingBaseDesign`. Alternatively, use the asset infra and a link.
C. **Separate design lab/preview app**: a page rendering all `pathland-*` components with the CSS from disk, using a live-reload dev server (Vite? but no runtime deps). Designers iterate there, then the CSS becomes the built-in or app base. This decouples design from app compilation. Could be a small static HTML + vanilla JS harness or a Rust/Java demo. But still need to get it into the renderer eventually.
D. **Move CSS to CSS files and generate the Rust `STYLE` at build time** via `include_str!` or a build script. This improves authoring but not the compile roundtrip. Combine with B for dev.

The real issue: "Every style has to be compiled into rust, but that is not suitable for a design flow." So the fix is to make the HTML renderer's base design a **runtime-loaded asset**, not a compile-time constant. The renderer should not be the authoring surface. Designers edit CSS; the renderer receives the CSS string (per app config) at render time.

Recommended direction:
1. **Extract the built-in CSS into a real `.css` file** (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/base.css` or similar), include it with `include_str!` for the built-in default. This makes CSS authoring first-class (syntax, tools). But production still compiles it.
2. **Add a runtime base design source**:
   - `BaseDesign` can be `embedded()` (include_str!), `inline(css, replace)`, or `file(path)` / `resource(classpath)`.
   - In dev, configure `BaseDesign.file(...)` or serve `/_pathland/base.css` from a disk dir. The renderer reads it per render (mtime cache) and emits it inline (or link).
   - Provide a "watch" mode: server watches the file and refreshes; browser reload. Could use a simple mtime check per request, no watcher needed. For live CSS without reload, the client could re-fetch, but plain reload is fine.
3. **Serve base CSS as an asset for pure CSS iteration**: Add a dev endpoint `GET /_pathland/base.css` that serves the current base CSS (from file or embedded). Emit `<link rel="stylesheet" href="{base}/_pathland/base.css">` in dev (configurable), and inline in prod. Or always emit link with content hash. The asset infrastructure already exists.
4. **Design lab**: optionally create a static "design lab" route/HTML that renders a representative sample tree (buttons, inputs, toggles, sliders, menus, etc.) so designers can see every component with the base CSS. This can be a small demo in the repo, maybe under `pathland-demo-views` or a new `design-lab` module. It should accept the CSS file and hot reload. This is the actual "design flow" ergonomics: edit CSS, see all components immediately.
   - Could leverage the existing demo (KitchenSink) but it requires app compile only once; CSS edits live. If the server loads CSS from disk at render time, `mvn quarkus:dev`/Spring devtools + browser refresh is enough. Quarkus dev mode already hot-reloads resources? If served from classpath, yes, but reading via `BaseDesign.fromFile` from `src/main/resources` path works.
   - For the library's own built-in design, a design lab in the Rust workspace could render `pathland-render-html` output with a CSS file passed via env var.

Need to think about SSR vs DOM client:
- If base CSS is inlined per render from a file, the DOM client gets it in the initial HTML. Good.
- If linked, the browser loads it; the DOM client doesn't need to know. Good.
- Live CSS reload: the browser reloads the page (or CSS-only HMR with a tiny script). We can propose a dev-only `<script>` or rely on browser refresh. Quarkus dev mode has live reload for resources and may trigger browser refresh; Spring devtools restarts. But if the server reads the CSS file per request, a browser refresh is enough even without server restart. For CSS-only changes, a browser extension (LiveReload) or a small dev script could reload the stylesheet. Keep it simple: refresh.

Important: The user's concern isn't just config; it's the loop. We should propose an explicit **design workflow**:
- `assets/base.css` is the source of truth.
- Dev: host points at that file (via `pathland.base-design` config or `BaseDesign.fromFile`), reads per render (mtime), link or inline; use `mvn quarkus:dev`/`spring-boot:run` with a design lab page; edit CSS → browser refresh.
- Prod: default embedded (include_str!), so no file dependency; or opt into link/custom CSS.
- No Rust rebuild for CSS changes in dev. In prod, built-in CSS changes require a release build (expected).

Should the base design live in Java/TS rather than Rust? The renderer is the right owner, but CSS shouldn't be compiled. Putting the file in the Rust crate (include_str!) and shipping it in the jar/dylib is still "compiled" for prod. For dev, runtime file wins.

Alternative: **Make base CSS an app-owned file entirely** (no built-in CSS in Rust), and ship a default CSS file alongside the renderer. The renderer just inserts whatever CSS it is given. This flips ownership: the HTML renderer has no built-in design; the default design is an asset. But that breaks "renderer owns defaults" and requires every host to provide CSS. Better: built-in fallback remains, but overridable.

Another key idea: **token layer vs component layer source files**. For design flow, split into:
- `tokens.css` (design tokens: colors, spacing, typography, radii, component token aliases)
- `components.css` (component rules)
- `reset.css`
A manifest or directory. Designers can work on tokens and component CSS separately. But a single base.css is simpler for now. Could still split physically and concatenate at build/runtime.

Let's inspect whether there are existing CSS files anywhere (maybe `lib/typescript` has base CSS?). Search for `.css` files.

Now think deeply about the design flow the user wants. "Every style has to be compiled into rust, but that is not suitable for a design flow." They likely want:
- Designers to edit CSS (and maybe HTML) and see changes immediately.
- No Rust recompile for each tweak.
- The base design system should be an artifact (CSS) that the renderer consumes, not code.

We need a plan for that. Since the previous plan was about "replace whole design system" via custom CSS, the user is now highlighting the **authoring/iteration loop** as the main concern. So the plan should center on runtime-loaded stylesheets + a design lab + dev workflow.

Key questions:
1. Should the base design be delivered as a **linked external stylesheet** (best for CSS hot reload) or **inlined per render from a file** (self-contained, no extra request, still no rebuild)?
2. What's the dev environment: Quarkus dev mode, Spring Boot devtools, or a standalone design lab?
3. Should the renderer's built-in CSS remain as a fallback/embedded default, or should there be no built-in? (Keep built-in.)
4. Should the CSS be split into tokens/components/reset files? Designers might want tokens separate.
5. Is live CSS hot reload (no full page refresh) needed, or is browser refresh acceptable? Big difference: link + HMR script vs. SSR inline.

Let me think about the architecture that best serves a design flow:

**Option 1: External `<link rel="stylesheet" href=".../base.css">`**
- Pros: Browser reloads CSS independently; with a small dev script or a tool like `browser-sync`, CSS hot-swaps without page reload. Standard design workflow. DevTools can live-edit CSS and persist back to file if using workspaces. No need to re-render SSR to see CSS changes.
- Cons: Extra request; SSR first paint depends on external CSS; the "no external stylesheets" test changes; CSP; need a stable URL (content hash in prod). The DOM client hydration is unaffected.
- Delivery: the host serves `/_pathland/base.css` from classpath/disk; dev config points to a file. The renderer emits the link when `BaseDesign::link(url)` is configured. Or always link (like most web apps) with a hashed URL for cache busting.
- This is probably the best "design flow": design CSS as a first-class asset. The renderer's built-in CSS becomes a default CSS file shipped in the jar/dylib (or served from the Rust crate via C ABI? For Java hosts, the CSS file can be in the Java module or served by Rust). Hmm, if the Rust renderer is the owner, it can serve the built-in CSS over the C ABI (`pathland_html_base_css`) and the host can serve it at `/_pathland/base.css`; in dev, the host serves a disk file instead. The HTML emits a link either way. This cleanly decouples CSS from Rust: the Rust renderer only emits the link/URL, not the CSS content. But then a Rust-native HTML host (is there one? maybe not) needs to serve the CSS separately. The current Rust HTML renderer is used via C ABI/SSR; the Java host serves assets. Could be fine.
- Potential issue: The renderer must know the URL. Per-app base design config includes the URL. `PathlandApp.baseDesign()` can return a URL or inline CSS. Default could be inline for standalone Rust use, link for Java server. That's complexity.

**Option 2: Inline CSS read from file per render**
- Pros: Self-contained, no FOUC, no extra request, no CSP issue. Still no Rust recompile; edit file, refresh page, new inline style.
- Cons: CSS changes require a full page reload (fine for most design work; SSR renders each request). Browser DevTools live-edit won't persist unless you have workspaces. Cannot hot-swap CSS only. Also reading file per render (cache with mtime) and inlining large CSS each SSR response increases payload. But it's likely small (~20KB).
- Delivery: `BaseDesign.fromFile(path)` with mtime-based caching, or a `Supplier<String>`. Host config.
- This is simpler and fits the existing "inline everything" decision (status.md: "inline-all + built-in design system"). It preserves the no-external-asset property. The design loop is: edit CSS file → browser refresh (server reads on each request). With Quarkus dev mode, refresh. No Rust/Java rebuild if the file is read at runtime (not classpath-cached). Could even add a tiny dev script that reloads the page on file change, but a manual refresh is enough.
- To get CSS-only hot reload, the dev server could poll the file and trigger a browser refresh via a dev script, but that's extra. Not necessary.

**Option 3: Build-time CSS file (include_str!) only**
- Not enough; user explicitly says compiled into Rust is unsuitable.

**Option 4: Design lab with live server**
- A dedicated page that renders representative components and loads CSS via link, with a watcher/live-reload. This gives designers a fast, contained loop. The lab could be a Rust demo (`pathland-design-lab`) that serves the HTML output and the CSS file, or a Java demo. Or a static page that uses SSR output snapshots. The key is to render *all* component classes and states so the CSS can be designed comprehensively.
- The design lab should not require the app to run (or it could reuse the demo). A minimal "component gallery" view in `pathland-demo-views` (Java DSL) plus the base CSS from disk would be ideal. But the lab needs a running server. Could be a `pathland-html-lab` crate/demo.
- Alternatively, generate a static gallery HTML at build/dev time from the renderer, and open the CSS in a browser. But changes to CSS are still picked up if linked.

What does "design system" include beyond CSS? The base design also includes the DOM structure the renderer emits (e.g. button markup, toggle markup, stepper composite). Designers can't change that via CSS alone. But the user specifically says "Every style has to be compiled into rust" — so they're focused on styles/CSS, not DOM. Fine.

Also, the token catalog is fixed; designers might want new tokens. The renderer's CSS can use arbitrary `--pl-*` variables, but `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` paths map via `token_spec.rs`. For a custom base design, they can define arbitrary variables in their CSS. Token paths outside the standard catalog are renderer-optional. Not the main issue.

- Move `css.rs` raw string to `assets/base.css` and `const CSS: &str = include_str!("../assets/base.css");`. This is a compile-time inclusion, but the file is a real CSS asset (tooling, formatting, linting). For dev, override via runtime file.

- Add a `PathlandApp.baseDesign()` default `BaseDesign.embedded()`. In dev, app returns `BaseDesign.fromFile(Path.of(".../base.css"))`. Or a config property `pathland.base-design.file` auto-wires it, so no code change. That's the best DX: set a property in `application.properties` (or env) pointing at the CSS file; the starter's `PathlandApp` wrapper (or `PathlandSession`) uses it. Now, let's think about how to make the design flow really good.

The user says "Every style has to be compiled into rust, but that is not suitable for a design flow." So the main ask: decouple CSS authoring from Rust compilation. A plan should propose:

1. **Move base CSS out of Rust source into a real CSS asset** (still included for the default), e.g. `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/base.css`, split into `reset.css`, `tokens.css`, `components.css` maybe.
2. **Runtime-loaded base design** with hot reload:
   - Rust: `BaseDesign::from_file(path)` with mtime cache; `render_document_with_base`.
   - C ABI: accept CSS string.
   - Java: `BaseDesign.fromFile(Path)` + auto-reload; `PathlandApp.baseDesign()`, plus starter config `pathland.base-design.file=...`.
3. **External stylesheet mode** (optional): `BaseDesign::linked(url)` emits `<link rel="stylesheet">`; host serves the file at `/_pathland/base.css`. This gives true CSS hot-swap (no full page reload) and makes design work native.
4. **Design lab**: a small component gallery page (all `.pathland-*` components and states) that runs under the dev server with the CSS file, so designers can iterate. It could be part of the demo or a dedicated `pathland-html-lab`.
5. **DX**: dev-only file watcher/browser refresh or live-reload. A tiny dev-only script injected when `base-design.watch=true` could poll/reload CSS. Or recommend Quarkus dev mode's live reload + browser refresh. Or use a standard tool (e.g. `npx live-server` or the IDE). The key is no rebuild.
6. **Production**: default embedded CSS; optionally link with content hash; no runtime file dependency. Provide a build step to snapshot the chosen design into the built-in CSS if it should become the default.

Maybe the cleanest "design flow" is actually a standalone **CSS-first workflow**:
- The base CSS file lives in the app/design repo: `design/base.css`.
- The renderer is configured with `pathland.base-design.file=...` in dev.
- The host serves `/_pathland/base.css` from that file (with no-cache in dev) and the SSR emits a `<link>` (or inline). Designers use browser devtools / live reload.
- For production, the same file is bundled (classpath resource or embedded) and served with a content hash.
- The Rust crate ships a default `assets/base.css` used when no file is configured; it can be forked and the app's file becomes the design.

But the user might want to design the renderer's *built-in* design, not just app-level. The plan should support both:
- Designers fork the default `base.css` and iterate on it via the runtime file; once done, it can either stay as the app's base design (per-app config) or be upstreamed into the crate's built-in default (copy back).
- A `pathland-design` / `design-lab` environment points at the local CSS.

Important question: Do they need **live reload without page refresh**, or is refresh enough? For CSS design, link + live reload is much nicer. But it adds complexity. I should ask.

Also: Is the design flow for the **HTML renderer's built-in design** (maintainers) or for **app teams branding their app**? The wording "design system for the html renderer" suggests maintainers/designers creating the default design system. In that case, a design lab in the Rust workspace + a CSS file loaded at runtime is the target. Maybe a small Rust binary `pathland-design-lab` that:
- Renders a gallery of all components via `pathland-render-html`.
- Serves the HTML and CSS from disk.
- Watches the CSS file and reloads.
No Java needed. Or a Java demo using the existing renderer.

Could add `pathland-html-design-lab` (Rust, tiny HTTP server? would need a dependency; or use a static file + `python -m http.server`?). The repo avoids new deps maybe. A Java demo is easier (Spring/Quarkus already). But a design lab for the renderer's own CSS should not require the Java stack; though it already exists and is the primary consumer.

Alternative: A **static gallery generator**: a Rust binary/test that emits a `gallery.html` from a representative opcode batch using `render_document`, with the CSS inlined from a file. Then designers open the file (no server) and use a browser auto-refresh extension. But SSR HTML is static; CSS changes require re-running the generator unless the CSS is linked. If the gallery links to `base.css`, designers can just refresh. That's simple: generate once, then edit CSS; no rebuild. The gallery can be a committed/dev artifact. But components with JS interactions (toggle/slider) won't be interactive; `render_document` output is static HTML with native controls, so some are interactive natively. Could be enough.

Better: the design lab is a **small page that loads the renderer's example tree** and links the CSS. It can be served by any static server.   - `Inline(String)` (replace flag)

**Phase B: Host integration (Java)**
- `BaseDesign` Java type with `embedded()`, `file(Path)`, `resource(String)`, `inline(css)`, `link(url)`, `replace`.
- `PathlandApp.baseDesign()` default embedded.

The base URL is only applied in `PathlandSession.renderHtml` by replacing `<html>`. The renderer's `render_document` doesn't know the base. For a link, it needs the URL. - `BaseDesign::link_file(path, url)` (optional, CSS hot reload; host serves it).
Choose one as default. Since the user said "roundtrip difficult", link mode with live reload might be the best experience. But it adds infrastructure. I'd recommend link mode for the design lab/dev, inline for production. Or inline-by-default with an opt-in link.

Wait, there's a subtlety with **the DOM client and token overrides**: The base CSS file can be linked; token overrides are still inline `<style data-pathland-tokens>`. Fine. The DOM client only needs the initial document. If CSS is linked, changing it in prod requires a new URL/hash. Fine.
